chapterName: Early Republic: The Samnite Wars (367-290 BCE)

briefing.title: Rome, 343 BC
paragraphs: It is 343 BC. Rome controls the land south to the River Liris. Beyond lies Campania, a fertile plain led by rich Capua. Above it, in the Apennine Mountains, live the Samnites, hill tribes and the strongest people in the region.

A treaty keeps Rome and the Samnites apart, but Samnite armies have penned the Campanians inside Capua, and desperate envoys are begging the Roman Senate for help. Three wars over the next fifty years will decide who dominates Italy.

timelines.name: Level 1: The Big Moments
timelines.blurb: Four turning points in Rome's long struggle with the Samnites.

events.label: Rome and the Samnites sign a treaty
events.fact: Livy and Diodorus record the treaty but not its terms; modern historians suspect it made the River Liris a dividing line.

events.label: Campanians surrender Capua to Rome
events.fact: After the Senate refused an alliance, Livy says the Campanian envoys handed Capua and all Campania to Rome unconditionally, dragging Rome into war.

events.label: Roman army trapped at the Caudine Forks
events.fact: The Samnite commander Gaius Pontius blocked both ends of the gorges and sent the Romans out unarmed under the yoke.

events.label: Decius Mus sacrifices himself
events.fact: At Sentinum the consul Decius Mus prayed to the gods and charged to his death, and his men rallied to break the coalition.

timelines.name: Level 2: Battles and Colonies
timelines.blurb: Victories, defeats and a new colony across three wars.

events.label: Valerius wins at Mount Gaurus
events.fact: The consul Marcus Valerius Corvus won near Cumae with a desperate charge as daylight faded.

events.label: Roman garrison mutinies in Campania
events.fact: Troops seduced by Campanian luxury plotted a coup, but Valerius, named dictator, talked them down without bloodshed.

events.label: Rome founds a colony at Fregellae
events.fact: The colony on the Liris lay in an area the Samnites had recently overrun, and they saw it as open aggression.

events.label: Samnites win at Lautulae
events.fact: When fighting resumed after a truce, the Samnites defeated Rome at Lautulae.

events.label: Romans capture Bovianum
events.fact: Bovianum was the capital of the Pentri, the largest Samnite tribe; the Samnites sued for peace the next year.

events.label: Papirius takes Aquilonia
events.fact: Tipped off by a deserter, the consul Papirius Cursor intercepted elite Samnite companies and took the town.

timelines.name: Level 3: The Long Road to Mastery
timelines.blurb: From the first peace to Rome's huge allied armies.

events.label: Old treaty renewed, Capua kept
events.fact: Rome left the Sidicini to the Samnites but kept its alliance with Capua, a far greater prize.

events.label: Naples opens its gates to Rome
events.fact: Two leading Neapolitans, fed up with the unruly Samnite garrison, let the Romans into the Greek city.

events.label: Luceria retaken, hostages freed
events.fact: Livy reports this Roman revenge after the Caudine Forks, though some historians doubt it.

events.label: Etruscans besiege Sutrium
events.fact: The Etruscans attacked Sutrium, which Rome saw as its key to Etruria, opening a second front.

events.label: Etruscan might broken at Lake Vadimo
events.fact: Livy says this hard-fought victory first broke the power of the Etruscan city-states.

events.label: Lucanians ask Rome for protection
events.fact: Their appeal against a Samnite invasion started the Third Samnite War.

events.label: Largest Roman colony founded at Venusia
events.fact: Venusia commanded routes into Lucania, Apulia and Samnium.

events.label: Rome and allies fight Gauls at Telamon
events.fact: The Greek historian Polybius counted about 41,000 Romans alongside 210,000 allies.

trueFalseDecks.name: The First War and Its Doubts
trueFalseDecks.blurb: How the first war began, and whether Livy got it right.

cards.claim: The River Liris divided Latium from Campania.
cards.why: The Liris separated Latium, the Latin homeland around Rome, from the fertile Campanian plain.

cards.claim: The Samnites spoke Latin, like the Romans.
cards.why: The Samnites spoke Oscan, an Italian language shared with several neighbours.

cards.claim: The first war began when the Samnites attacked the Sidicini.
cards.why: The Samnites attacked the Sidicini, a small people north of Campania; the Campanians helped them and were beaten.

cards.claim: The Senate eagerly accepted the Campanians' offer of alliance at once.
cards.why: Livy says the senators were tempted but refused, since an alliance would betray their treaty with the Samnites.

cards.claim: Valerius won at Mount Gaurus with a surprise charge at dawn.
cards.why: He won with a desperate charge as daylight faded.

cards.claim: In the peace of 341 BC Rome kept its alliance with Capua.
cards.why: Rome left the Sidicini to the Samnites but kept Capua, a far greater prize.

cards.claim: Livy's Campanian envoys give a speech modelled on a scene in Thucydides.
cards.why: It closely resembles Thucydides' scene where envoys from Corcyra beg Athens for help.

cards.claim: Salmon and Forsythe accept Capua's surrender in 343 BC as genuine.
cards.why: Salmon and Forsythe think it was invented, projected back from 211 BC; Cornell and Oakley are the ones who accept it.

trueFalseDecks.name: From the Caudine Forks to Mastery
trueFalseDecks.blurb: The second and third wars and what they built.

cards.claim: In 328 BC Rome founded a colony at Fregellae, on the Liris.
cards.why: The Samnites saw this colony, in an area they had recently overrun, as open aggression.

cards.claim: Naples was then an Etruscan city.
cards.why: Naples was a Greek city made up of an old town, Paleopolis, and a newer one, Neapolis.

cards.claim: Before the Caudine Forks, Samnite soldiers disguised as merchants spread a false rumour.
cards.why: They were disguised as shepherds, spreading the rumour that Luceria was under attack.

cards.claim: According to the story, Pontius chose the middle course his father warned against.
cards.why: Herennius said to free all the Romans or kill them all; Pontius let them go humiliated under the yoke.

cards.claim: Fabius sent his Etruscan-speaking brother through the Ciminian Forest disguised as a shepherd.
cards.why: After this scouting trip, Fabius marched his army through a forest no Roman had ever crossed.

cards.claim: At Sentinum, Gallic chariots broke the wing commanded by Fabius.
cards.why: The chariots broke Decius' wing; Decius then sacrificed himself, and Fabius outflanked the Samnites.

cards.claim: At Venusia Rome founded its largest colony ever.
cards.why: Rome took Venusia in 291 BC and settled its largest colony there, commanding routes into three regions.

cards.claim: At Telamon in 225 BC, Polybius counted more Romans than allies.
cards.why: He counted about 41,000 Romans alongside 210,000 allies.

oddOneOut.why: The Samnites, Etruscans and Umbrians (with the Senone Gauls) fought Rome together in 295 BC; the Lucanians had asked Rome for protection against the Samnites.
Cossus, Papirius and Carvilius were Roman consuls; Gaius Pontius was the Samnite commander at the Caudine Forks.
Diodorus, Polybius and Dionysius of Halicarnassus were Greek historians; Livy was Roman and wrote in Latin.
Rome won at Mount Gaurus, Suessula and Sentinum; at Lautulae in 315 BC the Samnites won.
Cales, Fregellae and Venusia received Roman colonists; Capua was the chief Campanian city and Rome's ally, not a Roman colony.
Consuls, dictators and proconsuls held power to lead armies; fetials were priests who handled formal demands and declarations of war.
The speech, the rescue and the assembly are suspected of being borrowed or invented; most historians now accept the war itself really happened.

whoAmI.name: Roman Commanders
whoAmI.blurb: Generals and heroes who fought the Samnites.

people.name: Marcus Valerius Corvus
clues: I rushed to Suessula on Campania's eastern edge and captured the enemy camp.
Named dictator in 342 BC, I talked mutinous soldiers down without bloodshed.
My desperate charge as daylight faded won Rome's first victory of the war.
I won the battle of Mount Gaurus, near Cumae.

people.name: Publius Decius Mus
clues: Historians suspect my famous exploit was borrowed from an episode of 258 BC.
I was only a junior officer when a consul was trapped in a mountain pass.
With a small band I seized a hilltop and distracted the enemy while the army escaped.
My son, who shared my name, gave his life at Sentinum.

people.name: Quintus Fabius Maximus Rullianus
clues: In 295 BC I shared the consulship with the son of an earlier war hero.
At Sentinum I outflanked the Samnites after my colleague died.
My Etruscan-speaking brother scouted ahead for me disguised as a shepherd.
I led the first Roman army through the dreaded Ciminian Forest.

people.name: Lucius Papirius Cursor
clues: Thanks to a deserter's tip, I intercepted twenty elite Samnite companies.
While my colleague took the surrender of Cominium, I attacked the town nearby.
One modern historian says my victory sealed the Samnites' fate.
I captured Aquilonia in 293 BC.

people.name: Gaius Pontius
clues: Later summaries say a Samnite commander of my name was paraded in a triumph and beheaded.
The story goes that I chose the middle course my father warned against.
I sent soldiers disguised as shepherds to spread a false rumour about Luceria.
I trapped two Roman consuls and their army at the Caudine Forks.

people.name: Herennius
clues: The story goes that I warned a middle course would neither win friends nor remove enemies.
My advice: free them all for friendship, or kill them all and cripple Rome.
As an elderly man, I was asked what to do with a trapped Roman army.
My son was the Samnite commander at the Caudine Forks.

people.name: Gellius Egnatius
clues: I knew my people could not beat Rome alone in the third war.
I helped bring Samnites, Etruscans, Umbrians and Gauls into one coalition.
A Roman raid drew home the Etruscans I had worked so hard to win over.
As Samnite commander, I took an army north to rally the Etruscans.
reviewFlags: fact-check: The chapter says only that Gellius Egnatius took an army north to rally the Etruscans; it does not credit him with bringing the Umbrians and Gauls into the coalition.

places.name: Capua
places.why: Campania's richest city, whose surrender to Rome in 343 BC, Livy says, started the First Samnite War.
reviewFlags: no coordinates on Wikipedia "Santa Maria Capua Vetere"; position is the model's estimate

places.name: Fregellae
places.why: Rome's colony on the Liris, founded in 328 BC, which the Samnites saw as open aggression.

places.name: Naples
places.why: The Greek city whose quarrel with Rome sparked the Great Samnite War and fell to a siege in 326 BC.

places.name: Caudine Forks
places.why: The Apennine gorges where the Samnites trapped a Roman army in 321 BC and sent it under the yoke.

places.name: Lake Vadimo
places.why: Site of the hard-fought victory of 310 BC that, Livy says, first broke Etruscan might.

places.name: Sentinum
places.why: East of the Apennines, where Rome defeated a coalition of four peoples in 295 BC.

places.name: Venusia
places.why: Taken in 291 BC and settled as Rome's largest colony ever, commanding routes into Lucania, Apulia and Samnium.
